Wanderers
won'der-erz
n. pl. (those who rove without a settled home; in Hosea, a people scattered under judgment)
From wander, Saxon wandrian, to rove, connected with wend and wind — to go by a turning, uncertain course. The word carries aimlessness in its root, not merely travel.

Biblical Definition

Both occurrences are judgments, and they run in opposite directions. Jeremiah, against Moab: “Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will send unto him wanderers, that shall cause him to wander, and shall empty his vessels, and break their bottles” (Jer 48:12). Moab had been settled on his lees, undisturbed from youth, never poured from vessel to vessel — and God sends wanderers to make him wander. The second is against Israel herself, and it is the severer of the two: “My God will cast them away, because they did not hearken unto him: and they shall be wanderers among the nations” (Hos 9:17). The cause is named exactly: they did not hearken. Wandering in Scripture is the standing penalty for a people who would not stay put under God's word, and the sentence goes back to Cain — “a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth” (Gen 4:12). But the Bible also has a wandering that is not a curse at all, and Hebrews is careful to distinguish it: the patriarchs “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13) — men without a settled country because they were looking for a better one. The difference is not the walking; it is whether a man is driven from a home or heading toward one.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines wanderer as one who roves; a rambler; one that deviates from duty; and wander as to rove; to ramble here and there without any certain course or object.

expand to see more

WAN'DERER, n. One that wanders; a rambler; one that roves; one that deviates from duty.

WAN'DER, v.i. [Sax. wandrian; from the root of wend, to go.]

1. To rove; to ramble here and there without any certain course or object in view.

2. To leave home; to depart; to migrate.

3. To depart from the subject in discussion. They shall be wanderers among the nations. Hos. 9.

Key Scripture

Hosea 9:17 — "My God will cast them away, because they did not hearken unto him: and they shall be wanderers among the nations."

Jeremiah 48:12 — "Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will send unto him wanderers, that shall cause him to wander, and shall empty his vessels, and break their bottles."

Genesis 4:12 — "When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth."

Hebrews 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

Modern Corruption

Rootlessness is now marketed as freedom, and the church has adopted the same restlessness under the name of following a call.

expand to see more

The culture has made a virtue of having no fixed place — the untethered life, the perpetual search, the refusal to settle — and Scripture consistently treats that condition as a judgment. Cain's sentence was to be a fugitive and a vagabond; Israel's was to be wanderers among the nations; and Moab's was to be poured from vessel to vessel after generations of comfortable stagnation. God does use dislocation to break settled complacency, as Jeremiah 48 shows. But wandering itself is never the goal, and a man who cannot stay anywhere has not achieved freedom.

The churchly version is transience dressed as guidance. Congregations are joined and left on preference, membership is treated as optional, and a believer may pass twenty years without ever being known well enough to be corrected. Hosea names the root cause of Israel's wandering, and it is not wanderlust: because they did not hearken unto him. Hebrews 11:13 keeps the one legitimate homelessness clearly marked — the patriarchs were strangers and pilgrims because they were persuaded of a promise and heading for a city. That is pilgrimage, which has a destination and usually a great deal of ordinary faithfulness in one place along the way. It is the opposite of drift.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nadad (H5074), to flee, wander; na wanad (H5128, H5110), fugitive and vagabond; Greek parepidemos (G3927), a resident foreigner, pilgrim.

expand to see more

Hebrew nodedim (H5074) — wanderers, fugitives; Hosea 9:17, of Israel among the nations.

Hebrew tso'im (H6808) — tilters, those who tip vessels; Jeremiah 48:12, the wanderers sent to pour Moab out.

Hebrew na wanad (H5128, H5110) — tottering and wandering; Genesis 4:12, Cain's sentence, and the root of the land of Nod.

Greek xenoi kai parepidemoi (G3581, G3927) — strangers and pilgrims; Hebrews 11:13, homelessness with a destination.

Saxon wandrian — to rove by a turning course; Webster's root, aimlessness built in.

Usage

"“They shall be wanderers among the nations” — and the cause is they did not hearken."

"“Wanderers, that shall cause him to wander” — Moab poured from vessel to vessel."

"“Strangers and pilgrims on the earth” — the one homelessness that is not a curse."
